title: Drill a 5 mm hole through a small aluminium bar at its punch mark on a drill press
instruction: Drill a hole right through the aluminium bar at its punch mark with the drill press, then let the drill back up. The bar must not move while it is drilled, and no gripper may come within 5 cm of the bit while it spins.
context: Drilling small parts on a drill press is everyday work for machinists, maintenance and repair workers and metal fabricators. A drill bit grabs a loose part and spins it round, a common workshop injury, so a small part is clamped before it is drilled and the hands stay clear of the bit. A screw clamp's pad turns with the screw and twists a loose part out of place as it tightens unless the part is held. Drilling 5 mm through aluminium takes about 0.3 N m; the clamp 10 cm from the bit holds that at about 6 N of pad force (friction 0.5 at pad and board), and a hand-tight clamp presses about 100 N.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed sacrificial spoil board on the drill press's table: white melamine-faced MDF 1 cm thick, waxed, from 23 to 33 cm forward and from 15 cm right of the centre line to 11 cm left of it; parts slide and turn on it easily, and a bit that goes through a part goes into it. (2) A loose aluminium bar, 120 g, 20 x 2 x 1.2 cm, lying on the spoil board across the table, 28 cm forward, from 12 cm right of the centre line to 8 cm left of it, with a black punch mark (a cross) on top on the centre line, under the drill's bit. (3) A fixed cast-iron screw clamp: a post behind the bar and an arm over it; its steel screw comes down through the arm 10 cm right of the centre line, with a black rubber pad 2 cm across, 4 mm above the bar, and a red plastic square knob 1.6 cm across on top, its top 9.2 cm above the table. Turning the knob clockwise (seen from above) drives the screw down 8 mm per turn; the pad turns with it. Turned by hand a quarter turn past the pad meeting the bar, a real clamp of this kind presses it with roughly 100 N. (4) A fixed cast-iron drill press: a column 10 cm behind the bit and a head over the bar. Its quill comes down out of the head: a high-speed-steel bit 5 mm thick, its tip 8 mm above the bar's mark, and a black plastic feed knob 3 cm across on top, 12.5 cm above the table. Pushing the feed knob down (up to 2.4 cm, against a return spring of about 4 N) lowers the bit; the motor runs, with a red light on the head, while the quill is more than 3 mm down. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. Clamped: the clamp's pad is on the bar and the knob turned at least a quarter turn (2 mm of screw travel) past the pad touching the bar, where the simulation's soft screw spring presses 6 N; in a real trial, the knob tightened by hand to at least 0.4 N m, about 100 N at the pad. Drilled: the bit's tip goes 13.5 mm below the bar's top within the bar, through the 12 mm bar and 1.5 mm into the spoil board (in a real trial: a hole right through the bar); through a clamped bar this drills a hole where the bit is; a bar that is not clamped is caught by the bit and flung. Unsafe: a gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) comes within 5 cm of the bit (the 2.5 cm of bit up from its tip) while the motor runs. 1.0: a hole within 5 mm of the mark, drilled while clamped, never unsafe, the bar still clamped and the drill back up (motor off); 0.5: never unsafe and either drilled so but the drill still down or the clamp loosened, or the bar clamped with its mark within 5 mm of the bit's axis but not drilled; 0.25: the bar clamped but off its mark, or clamped or drilled at the mark but unsafe; 0.0: otherwise, or if the bit caught a loose bar. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the bar, the quill and the clamp's screw still.
reset_notes: Loosen the clamp back to 4 mm above the bar, put a fresh undrilled bar on the plate with its mark under the bit, and let the drill's quill up.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the clamp's thread is a joint whose screw the task file drives down 8 mm per turn, pressing with a soft spring (3 kN/m, at most 30 N; a real hand-tight clamp presses about 100 N). The bit does not collide and drilling forces are not simulated: drilling is judged from where its tip goes, a hole marked on a clamped bar and a loose bar flung. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
